name: Femi Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for a side. This is confidential. What happens on a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the loading crew at Black Hollow, a large underground mine. I operate a scoop, which is a low machine that carries broken ore through the tunnels, then check each driver's route before we begin. My two-year technical diploma and years underground help me spot weak ground and unsafe shortcuts. I like getting everyone back to daylight; I dislike the new tablets and the noise after a long shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the job fit with life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jo and I have two children in school and a mortgage. The lead job pays well, we have more than six months of costs saved, and several other mines are within reach. I am the elected crew representative, so people bring me roster and safety concerns. I have never used an AI tool and would rather ask a person who has worked the tunnel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the loading machines are still ours to run, and I'd ask the company to fix the tunnel lights before buying another office program. If a form is faster, fine. I would take the safety concern to the next crew meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay looks steady and my skills still count. I do not enjoy the tablet work, but someone else can prepare the forms while I check the ground. Jo and I can meet the mortgage and keep our savings intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current loading roster and walk the access route with the drivers before each shift. At the next crew meeting I'd present the list of broken lights and ask for repair dates. I would keep our usual savings transfer each pay day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. There is still hard work and ordinary safety trouble, but I know how to deal with both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which light worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bend before the third loading bay is dark enough to hide a spill. I wrote it down with the shift date last week. A repaired light would do more for us than a cleaner form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jo about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Jo that our income stays much the same. We would keep the children in their activities and pay the mortgage as planned. I would still come home tired, but not worried about a missing wage.

say: I would demand **tunnel lights** before another office program while the loading machines stay staffed.
I would say **faster forms** are fine if the crew still checks the ground.
think: My **lead wage** and savings make the household secure in this picture.
I dislike **tablets**, though the paperwork change does not threaten my job.
do: Keep the **loading roster** and walk the access route with drivers each shift.
Raise **broken lights** at the crew meeting and request repair dates.
feel: **Calm** about income, with ordinary safety concerns.
S0.quote: A repaired light would do more for us than a cleaner form.
fieldNote: His **safety priority** is a specific dark bend, not a broad complaint about technology.
His **family cushion** makes the plateau feel financially secure despite the tiring shift.

steps.text: Keep leading the Black Hollow loading roster and access checks
Raise the dark loading bay at the next crew meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that software may take schedules and stock orders first, while underground loading changes more slowly. We should ask for a seat in any fleet discussion before shifts are cut. I would put that request in writing as the crew representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room might need fewer planners, and later a smaller loading crew could be enough. I am a strong operator, but the mine could still cut my lead post if the team shrinks. Other mines are nearby, yet their staffing might change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union branch for a written notice period before any loader trial. For the first year I'd keep working my shifts and collect the crew's safety observations about remote equipment. If my lead hours fell, I'd apply for a similar underground supervisor post at another mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can still act, but a smaller team could take away the pay our family plans around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the safety observations?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record blocked sight lines, damaged route markers and how long it takes a loader to stop on a wet floor. The crew already knows these things. I want a dated record before anyone promises a remote machine is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take remote control training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at a paid place if it led to a real post, but I would not volunteer for a screen course now. The operators already need time to make their cases. I would use my hours on that first.

say: I would seek a **fleet discussion** before any loading shifts are cut.
I would tell the crew that **planning tasks** change before hands-on loading does.
think: My **lead post** could disappear if the loading team becomes smaller.
Nearby **mine vacancies** offer options, though their staffing may change as well.
do: Request a **notice period** through the union branch before loader trials.
Record **crew safety observations** and apply elsewhere if my lead hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** because my own pay could shrink, with options still open.
S1.quote: I want a dated record before anyone promises a remote machine is safe.
fieldNote: His **crew record** captures measurable hazards around underground remote equipment.
He recognises **personal income risk** despite his skill and seniority.
He postpones **screen training** without claiming it could never help.

steps.text: Request trial notice terms at the next union branch meeting
Keep leading the underground loading shifts this year
Apply for nearby supervisor roles if lead hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 could write plans and schedules before it can move ore underground. The card puts capable hands-on robots around 2031. I would demand a crew vote on any new loading trial and paid protection for anyone whose hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side of my lead role could shrink by 2028, and the loading crew could face a hard cut around 2031. I expect I could lose a large part of my wage then, even if I stay for safety checks. Jo earns money too, and our reserve buys time, but losing the lead wage would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the planned extension to our house now and put the saved deposit toward the mortgage. In the first year after 2028 I'd ask the union for a wage protection clause and apply for a safety inspector vacancy if one opens at Black Hollow. I would not pay for a computer course with no job attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would lie awake thinking about the mortgage and the two children if the lead wage went. I could make a plan, but I would be angry at how little time the crew had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of the extension money is set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jo and I have set aside enough for the builder's first payment, about twelve thousand. I would ask Jo before moving it to the mortgage. The extra room can wait; the monthly loan bill is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for in a wage clause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would seek a year of protected pay while drivers move into another post, if the company agrees. I would also ask for paid time to train for actual vacancies. The union cannot promise those terms alone.

say: I would separate **2028 plans** from the 2031 hands-on robot risk.
I would demand **wage protection** and a crew say over loading trials.
think: I could lose **lead pay** by the robot date even if safety checks remain.
Jo’s wage and our **reserve** buy time, but they do not replace my mine income.
do: Delay the **house extension** and pay its deposit toward the mortgage after speaking with Jo.
Seek a **wage clause** and apply for an open safety inspector role after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about a major wage cut and the family mortgage.
S2.quote: The extra room can wait; the monthly loan bill is real.
fieldNote: He treats **2028 planning changes** and possible 2031 physical automation as different threats.
The **extension deposit** becomes a concrete debt payment only after Jo agrees.
His **union demand** is a proposal, not an assured company benefit.

steps.text: Delay the planned house extension this month
Pay the extension deposit toward the mortgage after Jo agrees
Seek wage protection at the union branch meeting
Apply for an open Black Hollow safety inspector job after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to negotiate before thinking work changes. Capable hands-on robots come around 2034 on the card, and no one should lose a shift without proper notice. I would ask for a posted fleet schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the first date and 51 at the robot date. Five years could bring the mortgage down, but I would still need work for many years. I would rather remain underground than learn a new screen, although I might have to consider safety inspections.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make two extra mortgage payments this year from our regular surplus, after Jo and I check the budget. I'd ask the union committee to propose a minimum notice period and a paid route into safety posts. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for an inspector vacancy if the mine actually advertises one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The years give us room to reduce debt, but I still see the team getting smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the inspector training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a paid place leads to a posted inspector vacancy, yes, I would take it. I will not spend family savings on an uncertain certificate. That is a practical line for me, even if I dislike the classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the younger loaders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the younger loaders to keep records of their equipment and safety work. I would bring their names into the union discussion on paid places. They should not be last in line because I have the loudest voice.

say: I would ask for **fleet notice** before any loading shift is removed.
I would mark **2031** for thinking work and **2034** for hands-on robots.
think: The **mortgage could shrink**, yet at 51 I would still need paid work.
I might need **safety inspection** work despite disliking screen training.
do: Make **two extra payments** on the mortgage this year if our budget allows.
Seek **notice terms** and apply for an advertised inspector vacancy after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer shifts, with more time to prepare.
S3.quote: I will not spend family savings on an uncertain certificate.
fieldNote: His **training condition** requires a paid place tied to a posted vacancy.
He uses **extra payments** to lower fixed costs while bargaining for his crew.

steps.text: Make two extra mortgage payments this year if the budget allows
Propose minimum fleet notice at the union committee
Apply for an advertised mine inspector role after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to make a proper agreement for every loading crew. Planning work may change in 2036, with capable hands-on robots around 2039. I would ask the union and mine to publish annual staffing numbers and funded training places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 when the robot date comes. If the mortgage is nearly gone and our savings keep growing, I might be able to reduce shifts before then. I cannot count on retiring early until Jo and I have checked the figures, and I worry about younger loaders who have no such cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the crew this year and ask the union committee to start an annual staffing review. I'd add another hundred to retirement contributions each pay day, then review the mortgage and pension with Jo each year. In the first year after 2036, if the numbers support it, I'd ask for fewer shifts rather than resign outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the crew, though calmer about my own income than in the faster pictures. A decade gives me a real chance to build a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What numbers would allow fewer shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would need the mortgage close to paid and enough retirement income to cover the gap until normal pension age. Jo and I would write the totals down together. I would not announce a retirement date from hope alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask for on behalf of younger loaders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want paid practice time on the new equipment and guaranteed interviews for open maintenance posts. A report that lists course seats and actual jobs would be useful. I would carry that request to the union committee.

say: I would press for **annual staffing figures** and funded practice places before 2039.
I would explain the **2036 planning** and 2039 hands-on dates to the loading crew.
think: Our **mortgage and pension** could allow fewer shifts if the figures support it.
Younger loaders may face **income loss** without my family cushion.
do: Keep **leading shifts** this year and request annual staffing reviews through the union.
Add **another hundred** to retirement each pay day and check the mortgage and pension with Jo annually.
feel: **Uneasy** for colleagues, but my own income has a possible bridge.
S4.quote: I would not announce a retirement date from hope alone.
fieldNote: His **reduced-shift plan** stays conditional on pension and mortgage figures.
He seeks **real job outcomes** for younger colleagues, with a dated report the mine can be held to.

steps.text: Keep leading Black Hollow loading shifts this year
Request annual staffing reviews through the union committee
Add another hundred to retirement contributions each pay day

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because planning could change quickly and the loading crew could lose shifts around 2031. A written fleet schedule, wage protection if posts go, and paid routes into actual safety jobs would help. I would still need the company to agree, not just the union to ask.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I wish you had asked what happens to the young loaders who are renting and have no reserve. I can put money against our mortgage; they cannot do the same. I represent young loaders with no savings as much as I represent experienced drivers.

headlineQuote: I represent young loaders with no savings as much as I represent experienced drivers.
portrait: **Femi Wagner**, 43, leads an underground loading crew and operates a scoop at a large mine.
His **technical diploma** and strong operating skill underpin good pay, substantial savings, a mortgage and two school-age children.
A **union representative**, he records safety hazards and seeks paid protections for colleagues; he has never used AI tools.
Fast AGI alarms him over **lead wages**; longer timelines allow debt reduction and possible fewer shifts if household figures support it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could change planning quickly and threaten loading shifts around the 2031 robot date.
whatWouldHelp: A **written fleet schedule**, agreed wage protection and paid entry into actual safety jobs would give his crew options.
